The Strait of Istanbul, connecting the Black Sea and the Marmara Sea, is a narrow and winding waterway that is often subject to incidents where ships enter harbors and sink.

The Strait of Istanbul is 29.9 kilometers long and is much narrower and more winding than the shipping lanes it serves. The strait's two shores are closest at the point between Anadolu Hisarı and Rumelihisarı, which is 698 meters apart. The deepest part of the strait is between the neighborhoods of Bebek and Kandilli, with a depth of 110 meters, and the second deepest part is between Arnavutköy and Vaniköy, with a depth of 106 meters. The average depth is 60 meters, and it increases from the south to the north.

The Strait of Istanbul's winding and narrow structure is evident throughout its entire length. The strait has 12 sharp bends, with bend angles of 45 degrees at Kandilli and 80 degrees at Yeniköy. Due to its winding structure, the length of the strait is not the same as the length of its shores. The length of the strait is 55 kilometers on the European side and 35 kilometers on the Asian side.

The shores of the strait are not flat and have steep cliffs. Many small hills can be found throughout the strait, especially on the European side. The most important hills are the 252-meter-high Büyük Çamlıca Hill and the 216-meter-high Küçük Çamlıca Hill.

The climate of the Strait of Istanbul is typically Mediterranean. The summers are hot and humid due to the presence of tropical and subtropical high-pressure systems. However, the summers in Istanbul are not as hot and long as they are in the west and south of Turkey. The climate in some parts of the strait can change seasonally due to local factors such as temperature and vegetation. The annual average temperature in the strait ranges between 13.6°C and 13.9°C. The average annual precipitation in the region ranges between 672 mm and 745 mm. The relative humidity in the region is typically between 70% and 80%, which is the highest recorded in Turkey. Sometimes, cold air masses can cause frost in the strait and its surroundings.

Foggy conditions are common in the strait, especially in the months of March and April. The strait can be closed to shipping due to fog or snow. Weather observations in the strait are made at the Kandilli Observatory, which is located at an altitude of 114 meters and is not able to make some measurements due to its location.

There is a parallel alignment between the two shores of the strait, starting from the south and passing through Dolmabahçe on the entrance side, Ortaköy on the exit side, Kandilli Burnu on the Bebek side, Yeniköy on the Paşabahçe side, and so on. However, the distribution of ports and bays is not equal on both shores. The most important ports and bays on the European side are 1781 in number, while on the Asian side there are 3434 ships, including fishing boats and private yachts. Most of these ships are fishing boats and are concentrated in the northern part of the strait due to the migration of fish during the season. The distribution of fishing areas is 74 in Rumelikavağı, 30 in Sarıyer, and 20 in İstinye on the European side, and 91 in Anadolukavağı, 8 in Yalıköy, and 27 in Anadoluhisarı on the Asian side.

The two islands surrounded by the strait are called Kız Kulesi (Maiden's Tower) and Kuruçeşme Adası (Kuruçeşme Island). The island located on the Marmara Sea side, which is above Kız Kulesi, is officially known as Kuruçeşme Adası. The island is located approximately 100 meters from the Salacak coast.
